content_units: 2016 Honda Civic Rough Idle: Likely Faults at 118,000 km

Your symptoms point most strongly to a   combustion/air-fuel issue   rather than a major engine failure: rough idle at stops, hesitation on acceleration, worse fuel economy, and an intermittent check-engine light. Short city trips also increase the odds of   carbon buildup, dirty airflow components, weak ignition parts, and battery/charging-related low-voltage behavior  .
Most plausible causes, ranked for your symptom pattern and budget:
Likely Cause   Why it fits   Typical diagnostic clue   Usual repair priority   Typical CAD range

Dirty or failing spark plugs / ignition coil issue   Misfire causes rough idle, hesitation, poorer fuel economy, flashing/intermittent CEL   Misfire codes such as P0300-P0304; roughness under load     High     180-500

Carbon buildup on throttle body / intake path   Common with short-trip driving; can cause unstable idle and poor throttle response   Dirty throttle plate, unstable idle, improved idle after cleaning     High     120-250
Vacuum leak / intake air leak   Lean mixture can create rough idle, hesitation, fuel trim issues   High positive fuel trims, hiss, smoke-test leak     High     120-350

Dirty or weak fuel injector(s)   Can cause rough idle, hesitation, and mpg drop without smoke/overheating   Cylinder contribution imbalance, misfire on one cylinder, injector pattern issue     Medium-High     150-450

MAF/MAP sensor contamination or sensor reading error   Bad airflow/load signal affects fueling and throttle response   Fuel trims off, implausible sensor readings on scan tool     Medium-High     100-300
PCV valve issue   Can upset idle quality and increase oil vapor/carbon effects   Idle quality changes, crankcase vacuum abnormal     Medium     80-180
Weak battery / charging voltage irregularity   Hondas can idle poorly or behave oddly if voltage is unstable, especially on short trips   Low resting voltage, charging below spec     Medium     0-300

Early injector, pump, or high-pressure fuel delivery issue   Fits hesitation and mpg loss, but usually diagnosed after basics   Fuel pressure/performance faults, lean under load     Medium     250-700+
First Diagnostic Steps a Mechanic Should Do
Start with the highest-yield, lowest-cost checks before replacing parts.
Step   Action   What to Check   Expected Result
1   Full OBD-II scan with stored/history/pending codes   Misfire, fuel trim, airflow, injector, catalyst, voltage codes   Clear direction even if CEL is off now
2   Live-data review at idle and light throttle   Short/long fuel trims, misfire counters, coolant temp, O2/A/F sensor behavior   Identify lean, rich, or misfire pattern
3   Inspect ignition system   Plug wear, coil condition, oil in plug wells, connector fit   Worn plugs or weak coil often show early
4   Check intake system and throttle body   Dirty throttle plate, loose hose, cracked intake tube, air leak   Idle instability source often visible
5   Smoke test for vacuum leaks   PCV lines, intake manifold gasket, hose leaks   Confirms or rules out lean idle cause
6   Battery/charging test   Resting voltage, charging output, load-test result   Rules out low-voltage drivability issues
7   Fuel system review   Injector balance, pressure/performance if needed   Done after ignition/air checks if symptoms remain
Best Use of a CAD 700 Budget
Highest-priority fixes
These are the items most worth doing first because they best match your symptoms and usually give the best value.
Option 1:   Scan + live-data diagnosis     Finds the real direction before parts swapping   Best first spend
Book diagnosis
Option 2:   Replace spark plugs if due / inspect coils     Common cause of rough idle, hesitation, and mpg drop   High symptom match
Service info
Option 3:   Throttle body and intake cleaning; inspect air path     Especially worthwhile with frequent short trips   Strong idle-quality payoff
Find local shop
Option 4:   Smoke test and repair any vacuum leak / PCV issue     High-value if trims show lean running   Prevents wasting money on sensors
Repair network
Lower-priority or optional fixes
These are worth considering only after the first diagnostics or if evidence points there.
Option 1:   Injector cleaning service     Can help if one cylinder is weak or spray pattern is poor   Useful, but not always first-line
Compare service
Option 2:   MAF/MAP sensor cleaning or replacement     Good only if scan data supports it   Avoid blind replacement
Sensor basics
Option 3:   Battery replacement     Worth it if testing shows weak voltage from repeated short-trip use   Secondary unless test fails
Battery guide
Practical Repair Order for Your Case
A sensible under-budget sequence:
-   Step 1:   OBD scan + live data + basic visual inspection
Estimated:   CAD 120-180
-   Step 2:   Replace spark plugs if overdue; inspect/swap suspect coil only if indicated
Estimated:   CAD 180-350
-   Step 3:   Throttle body cleaning + intake inspection
Estimated:   CAD 120-220
-   Step 4:   Smoke test for vacuum leaks / PCV check
Estimated:   CAD 100-200
That puts many real-world cases in the   CAD 420-700   range, depending on whether coils or a leak repair are needed.
What This Most Likely Is
Given your exact symptom set, the strongest first suspects are:
-   Ignition-related misfire   from worn plugs or a weak coil
-   Dirty throttle body / intake-related idle instability
-   Vacuum leak or PCV-related lean idle
-   Injector or sensor issue   if the first three check out
Less likely from what you described:
- Head gasket
- Major internal engine damage
- Cooling system fault
- Serious oil-burning issue
